cases.title: Pitch-matching error in singers and non-musicians
cases.context: In a study looking at vocal pitch control, ten trained choir singers and ten non-musicians each heard a sung target note and sang it back. The pitch-matching error (the absolute distance between the sung note and the target) was recorded in cents (one hundredth of a semitone). The researchers wanted to know whether the errors in each group could be treated as Normally distributed before choosing a test.
tasks: For each group, calculate the mean, the SD, and the percentage of values within one SD and within two SDs of the mean, and compare them with the percentages expected for a Normal distribution.
Give the theoretical quantiles that qqnorm() uses for the smallest and the largest of the ten points.

For the trained singers, shapiro.test(x) in R printed "W = 0.98879, p-value = 0.9951". For the non-musicians it printed "W = 0.76707, p-value = 0.005761". State the hypotheses, the decision at the 0.05 level, and whether a parametric test such as the t test is appropriate for each group.

hypotheses.null: H_0:\text{the data come from a Normal distribution}
hypotheses.alternative: H_A:\text{the data do not come from a Normal distribution}
hypotheses.nullWords: There is no difference between the distribution of the data and a Normal distribution.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The distribution of the data differs from a Normal distribution.

cases.symbols: \(\bar x\) (sample mean), \(s\) (sample SD), \(p_i\) (plotting probability), \(z_i\) (theoretical Normal quantile), \(W\) (Shapiro-Wilk statistic), \(P\) (P value).

steps.title: State the procedure and hypotheses
general: H_0:\text{the data come from a Normal distribution}
H_A:\text{the data do not come from a Normal distribution}
steps.words: Normality is checked with the percentage of data in a range, the Normal Q-Q plot, and the Shapiro-Wilk test, one group at a time. The null hypothesis is that there is no difference between the distribution of the data and a Normal distribution.

steps.title: Mean and SD of the trained singers
steps.words: Add the ten values and divide by 10, then square each deviation, add them, divide by n - 1 = 9 and take the root.

steps.title: Percentages of the trained singers within one and two SDs
steps.words: Seven of the ten values (10, 11, 12, 13, 13, 14, 16) lie within one SD of the mean. This is 70% against the Normal 68.26%. All ten values lie within two SDs, close to the Normal 95.44%.

steps.title: Theoretical quantiles for qqnorm()
steps.words: For ten or fewer points R uses these plotting probabilities. The ten theoretical quantiles run from -1.54664 to +1.54664 and are the horizontal axis of the Q-Q plot. Each group's sorted values are plotted against them.

steps.title: Shapiro-Wilk result for the trained singers
steps.words: The P value is far above 0.05, so Normality is not rejected for the trained singers. The data are consistent with a Normal distribution. The Q-Q plot of the singers lies close to a straight line. A parametric test can be used for this group.

steps.title: Mean, SD and range percentages of the non-musicians
steps.words: Eight of the ten values (15, 18, 20, 22, 25, 28, 34, 45) lie within one SD of the mean. This is 80% against the Normal 68.26%. Nine values lie within two SDs (90% against the Normal 95.44%) because 110 lies beyond two SDs.

steps.title: Shapiro-Wilk result for the non-musicians
steps.words: The P value is below 0.05 (and below 0.01), so Normality is rejected for the non-musicians. On the Q-Q plot the non-musicians bend upward away from the line at the right end, the positive-skew pattern of a long right tail. A rank-based test is preferred for these data.

cases.conclusion: The trained singers give W = 0.98879 with P = 0.9951, so Normality is not rejected and the data are consistent with a Normal distribution. The non-musicians give W = 0.76707 with P = 0.005761, so Normality is rejected and the data are not Normal. So a t test is reasonable for the singers alone, but a comparison that includes the non-musicians should use a rank-based test.

steps.words: Nine of the ten values (0.28, 0.36, 0.41, 0.45, 0.49, 0.52, 0.58, 0.63, 0.69) lie within one SD of the mean. This is 90% against the Normal 68.26%. Nine values lie within two SDs (90% against the Normal 95.44%) because 1.92 lies beyond two SDs.

cases.title: Lever presses in extinction after two reinforcement schedules
cases.context: Researchers interested in animal learning did a study to evaluate how the training schedule affects extinction (the decline of a learned response once it is no longer rewarded). Rats were trained to press a lever for food pellets. Five rats were trained on continuous reinforcement (CRF, every press rewarded) and seven different rats on partial reinforcement (only some presses rewarded). In a 20-minute extinction session with no food, the number of lever presses was counted. The counts were skewed, so the researchers did not want to assume Normal populations.
tasks: Rank all 12 counts together, using average ranks for ties, and compute T for the smaller group.

Based on the recorded data, is there evidence that the number of lever presses in extinction is different in these two groups? Do not assume that the counts are Normally distributed. Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.

Provide your result in a single complete sentence that would convey your conclusion in a way that could be understood by a non-expert in statistics or medicine (e.g., a typical reader of a local newspaper).

hypotheses.null: H_0:\text{same distribution of extinction presses for CRF and partial}
hypotheses.nullWords: There is no difference in the distributions of lever presses in extinction between the CRF and partial reinforcement groups.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The distributions of lever presses in extinction differ between the CRF and partial reinforcement groups.

cases.symbols: \(T\) (sum of ranks in the smaller group), \(n_S\) (size of the smaller group), \(n_B\) (size of the bigger group), \(\mu_T\) (mean of \(T\) under the null hypothesis), \(\sigma_T\) (standard deviation of \(T\) under the null hypothesis), \(z_T\) (standardized rank sum).

steps.title: State the procedure and hypotheses
general: H_0:\text{the two population distributions are the same}
steps.words: The groups contain different rats and the bigger group has 7, so the procedure is the Mann-Whitney rank-sum test with the T table. The null hypothesis is that there is no difference in the distributions of lever presses in extinction between the two groups.

steps.title: Rank all observations with ties
general: \text{tied rank}=\text{average of the ranks the tied values occupy}
steps.words: All 12 values are ranked in one list regardless of group. Tied values each receive the average of the ranks they occupy, which applies to the two values of 22 and the two values of 29.

steps.title: Compute T
steps.words: The CRF group is the smaller group, so T is the sum of its 5 ranks. The two rank sums together must equal the total of the ranks 1 to 12.

steps.title: Describe the null distribution of T
steps.words: Under the null hypothesis each of the 792 sets of 5 ranks is equally likely. The rank sums are centered at 32.5.

steps.title: Read the critical values
steps.words: Open MannWhitney_RankSumT_Table.pdf, PDF page 1, row n_S = 5, n_B = 7. Near .05 the printed critical values are 20 and 45 with P = .048, and near .01 they are 17 and 48 with P = .010.

steps.title: Make the decision and bracket P
steps.words: T = 18 is at or below the lower value 20, so the null hypothesis is rejected. It does not reach the .01 lower value of 17, so 0.010 < P < 0.048.

cases.conclusion: T = 18 is at or below the lower critical value of 20, so the null hypothesis is rejected (0.010 < P < 0.048). There is a difference in lever presses in extinction between the two groups. Rats trained with partial reinforcement kept pressing the lever more often once food stopped than rats rewarded for every press.

cases.title: Stuttered syllables after two fluency therapies
cases.context: In a clinical trial on stuttering, adults who stutter were randomly assigned to fluency shaping (a therapy that teaches slow and smooth speech) or to stuttering modification (a therapy that teaches easier and shorter stutters). After 8 weeks of therapy each person read the same 200-syllable passage aloud, and the number of stuttered syllables (syllables with a repetition, prolongation or block) was counted. Four people completed fluency shaping and seven completed stuttering modification.
tasks: Rank all 11 counts together, using average ranks for ties, and compute T for the smaller group.

Based on the recorded data, is there evidence that the number of stuttered syllables is different in these two groups? Do not assume that the counts are Normally distributed. Please state how you reached your conclusions.

Provide your result in a single complete sentence that would convey your conclusion in a way that could be understood by a non-expert in statistics or medicine (e.g., a typical reader of a local newspaper).

hypotheses.null: H_0:\text{same distribution of stuttered syllables for both therapies}
hypotheses.nullWords: There is no difference in the distributions of stuttered syllables between the fluency shaping and stuttering modification groups.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The distributions of stuttered syllables differ between the fluency shaping and stuttering modification groups.

cases.symbols: \(T\) (sum of ranks in the smaller group), \(n_S\) (size of the smaller group), \(n_B\) (size of the bigger group), \(\mu_T\) (mean of \(T\) under the null hypothesis), \(\sigma_T\) (standard deviation of \(T\) under the null hypothesis), \(z_T\) (standardized rank sum).

steps.title: State the procedure and hypotheses
general: H_0:\text{the two population distributions are the same}
steps.words: The groups contain different people and the bigger group has 7, so the procedure is the Mann-Whitney rank-sum test with the T table. The null hypothesis is that there is no difference in the distributions of stuttered syllables between the two groups.

steps.title: Rank all observations with ties
general: \text{tied rank}=\text{average of the ranks the tied values occupy}
steps.words: All 11 values are ranked in one list regardless of group. Tied values each receive the average of the ranks they occupy, which applies to the two values of 9.

steps.title: Compute T
steps.words: The fluency shaping group is the smaller group, so T is the sum of its 4 ranks. The two rank sums together must equal the total of the ranks 1 to 11.

steps.title: Describe the null distribution of T
steps.words: Under the null hypothesis each of the 330 sets of 4 ranks is equally likely. The rank sums are centered at 24.

steps.title: Read the critical values
steps.words: Open MannWhitney_RankSumT_Table.pdf, PDF page 1, row n_S = 4, n_B = 7. Near .05 the printed critical values are 13 and 35 with P = .042, and near .01 they are 10 and 38 with P = .012.

steps.title: Make the decision
steps.words: T = 21.5 lies strictly between 13 and 35, so the null hypothesis is not rejected. Counting the equally likely rank sets with these tied ranks, 226 of the 330 are at least as far from 24 as T = 21.5, so the exact two-tailed P is 0.684848.

cases.conclusion: T = 21.5 lies between the critical values 13 and 35, so the null hypothesis is not rejected (P = 0.685). These data do not show that one therapy leaves people with fewer stuttered syllables than the other.

cases.title: Dizziness ratings after vestibular rehabilitation
cases.context: In a clinical trial on chronic dizziness, adults with a vestibular disorder (a problem of the balance organs of the inner ear) were randomly assigned to an 8-week vestibular rehabilitation course (home exercises of head and eye movements that retrain balance) or to a waitlist. At the end of the 8 weeks each person walked down a hallway while turning the head from side to side and rated dizziness on a 0 to 10 scale (0 = no dizziness, 10 = the worst dizziness imaginable). Nine people completed the rehabilitation course and eleven were on the waitlist. The ratings are ordinal and contain many ties.
tasks: Rank all 20 ratings together, using average ranks for ties, and compute T for the smaller group.

Based on the recorded data, is there evidence that the dizziness rating is different in these two groups? The ratings are ordinal, so do not assume that they are Normally distributed. Use the Normal approximation and correct for ties.

Provide your result in a single complete sentence that would convey your conclusion in a way that could be understood by a non-expert in statistics or medicine (e.g., a typical reader of a local newspaper).

hypotheses.null: H_0:\text{same distribution of dizziness ratings for rehabilitation and waitlist}
hypotheses.nullWords: There is no difference in the distributions of dizziness ratings between the rehabilitation and waitlist groups.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The distributions of dizziness ratings differ between the rehabilitation and waitlist groups.

cases.symbols: \(T\) (sum of ranks in the smaller group), \(n_S\) (size of the smaller group), \(n_B\) (size of the bigger group), \(\mu_T\) (mean of \(T\) under the null hypothesis), \(\sigma_T\) (standard deviation of \(T\) under the null hypothesis), \(z_T\) (standardized rank sum). \(\tau_i\) (number of tied ranks in the \(i\)th set of ties). \(N\) (total number of observations).

steps.title: State the procedure and hypotheses
general: H_0:\text{the two population distributions are the same}
steps.words: The two groups contain different people and the data are ordinal ratings with many ties, so the procedure is the Mann-Whitney rank-sum test. The null hypothesis is that there is no difference in the distributions of dizziness ratings between the two groups.

steps.title: Rank all 20 values and compute T
steps.words: All 20 values are ranked in one list, and tied values receive the average of the ranks they occupy. The rehabilitation group is the smaller group, so T is the sum of its ranks.

steps.title: Choose the Normal approximation
steps.words: The bigger group has more than 8 observations, so the T table does not apply and T is treated as Normal.

steps.title: Mean of T
steps.words: This is the rank sum expected for the rehabilitation group if there is no difference between the groups.

steps.title: Tie sum
steps.words: There are two sets of size 2, three sets of size 3 and one set of size 4. Each set of size \(\tau_i\) adds \((\tau_i-1)\tau_i(\tau_i+1)\).

steps.title: Tie-corrected standard deviation of T
steps.words: The ties reduce the variance of T from 173.25 to 170.124, so the standard deviation drops from 13.1624 to 13.0431.

steps.title: Compute z_T
steps.words: The continuity correction subtracts one half from the distance between T and its mean before dividing by the standard deviation.

steps.title: Read the critical value
steps.words: Start with \(\alpha=0.05\). Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 2. In the infinity row and the two-tailed 0.05 column, the printed value is 1.9600.

steps.title: Make the decision and bracket P
steps.words: The statistic exceeds 1.96, so the null hypothesis is rejected. In the infinity row it passes the 0.01 column (2.5758) but not the 0.005 column (2.8070), so 0.005 < P < 0.01.

cases.conclusion: T = 58.5 gives z_T = 2.72174, which exceeds 1.9600, so the null hypothesis is rejected (0.005 < P < 0.01). There is a difference in dizziness ratings between the two groups. People who completed vestibular rehabilitation reported less dizziness during head turns than people on the waitlist.

cases.title: Freezing time in mice with and without extinction training

On the next day each mouse heard the tone for 5 minutes and freezing time (complete stillness except for breathing) was recorded in seconds (s). Ten mice had extinction training and twelve did not. Freezing times were skewed to the right, with a few very long times.
tasks: Rank all 22 freezing times together, using average ranks for ties, and compute T for the smaller group.

Based on the recorded data, is there evidence that freezing time is different in these two groups? Do not assume that the freezing times are Normally distributed. Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.

Provide your result in a single complete sentence that would convey your conclusion in a way that could be understood by a non-expert in statistics or medicine (e.g., a typical reader of a local newspaper).

hypotheses.nullWords: There is no difference in the distributions of freezing time to the tone between mice with and without extinction training.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The distributions of freezing time to the tone differ between mice with and without extinction training.

steps.words: All 22 values are ranked in one list, and tied values receive the average of the ranks they occupy. The extinction group is the smaller group, so T is the sum of its ranks.

steps.words: The bigger group has more than 8 observations, so the T table does not apply and T is treated as Normal.

steps.title: Mean of T
steps.words: This is the rank sum expected for the extinction group if there is no difference between the groups.

steps.title: Tie sum
steps.words: There is one set of size 2. Each set of size \(\tau_i\) adds \((\tau_i-1)\tau_i(\tau_i+1)\).

steps.title: Tie-corrected standard deviation of T
steps.words: The ties reduce the variance of T from 230 to 229.87, so the standard deviation drops from 15.1658 to 15.1615.

steps.title: Compute z_T
steps.words: The continuity correction subtracts one half from the distance between T and its mean before dividing by the standard deviation.

steps.title: Read the critical value
steps.words: Start with \(\alpha=0.05\). Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 2. In the infinity row and the two-tailed 0.05 column, the printed value is 1.9600.

cases.title: Tic counts before and after habit reversal training
cases.context: In a study looking at Tourette syndrome (a disorder with sudden, repeated movements or sounds called tics), nine patients were video-recorded for 5 minutes while seated at rest, and the number of tics was counted. Each patient was evaluated before 3 weeks of habit reversal training (practice in noticing the urge that comes before a tic and making a competing movement instead) (measurement 1) and again after it (measurement 2). Tic counts are small integers and are not Normally distributed.
tasks: Compute the differences (after - before), drop any zero difference, rank the magnitudes with average ranks for ties, attach the signs and compute W.

Based on the recorded data, is there evidence that the number of tics is different in these two states? Do not assume that the differences are Normally distributed. Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.

Provide your result in a single complete sentence that would convey your conclusion in a way that could be understood by a non-expert in statistics or medicine (e.g., a typical reader of a local newspaper).

hypotheses.null: H_0:\text{no difference in tic counts before and after training}
hypotheses.alternative: H_A:\text{tic counts differ before and after training}
hypotheses.nullWords: There is no difference in the distributions of tic counts before and after habit reversal training.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The distributions of tic counts differ before and after habit reversal training.

cases.symbols: \(W\) (sum of the signed ranks), \(n\) (number of nonzero differences), \(\mu_W\) (mean of \(W\) under the null hypothesis), \(\sigma_W\) (standard deviation of \(W\) under the null hypothesis), \(z_W\) (standardized signed-rank sum).

steps.title: State the procedure and hypotheses
steps.words: Each patient is measured twice, so the procedure is the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. The null hypothesis is that there is no difference in the distributions of tic counts before and after habit reversal training.

steps.title: Drop the zero difference
steps.words: Patient 2 has no change, so that difference is dropped and n becomes 8. The W table applies.

steps.title: Rank the magnitudes and attach signs
steps.words: Tied magnitudes share the average of the ranks they occupy. Each rank then takes the sign of its difference.

steps.title: Compute W
steps.words: The positive ranks add to 1.5 and the negative ranks add to 34.5.

steps.title: Read the critical value
steps.words: Open WilcoxonW_Table.pdf, PDF page 1, row n = 8. The printed critical values are 32 with P = .024 and 28 with P = .054. The value 32 is the one whose P does not exceed 0.05.

steps.title: Make the decision and bracket P
steps.words: The magnitude 33 reaches the critical value of 32, so the null hypothesis is rejected. It is beyond the largest printed critical value for n = 8, so P < 0.024.

cases.conclusion: W = -33 with n = 8, and |W| = 33 reaches the critical value of 32, so the null hypothesis is rejected (P < 0.024). There is a difference in tic counts before and after habit reversal training. Patients had fewer tics during the 5-minute recording after three weeks of habit reversal training than before it.

cases.title: Mood ratings before and after a group music session

steps.words: Tied magnitudes share the average of the ranks they occupy. Each rank then takes the sign of its difference.

steps.title: Compute W
steps.words: The positive ranks add to 24 and the negative ranks add to 4.

steps.title: Read the critical value
steps.words: Open WilcoxonW_Table.pdf, PDF page 1, row n = 7. The printed critical values are 28 with P = .016 and 24 with P = .046. Both P values are at most 0.05, so 24 (P = .046) is the cutoff at the 0.05 level and 28 (P = .016) is a stricter cutoff.

steps.words: No difference is zero, so n stays 12. With more than 8 nonzero differences the Normal approximation is used.

steps.title: Rank the magnitudes with ties
general: \text{tied rank}=\text{average of the ranks the tied values occupy}
steps.words: Tied magnitudes share the average of the ranks they occupy, and each rank then takes the sign of its difference. The very large change of 9.8 for subject 10 gets the top rank of 12, so it cannot pull W further than any other largest value would.

steps.title: Compute W
steps.words: The positive ranks add to 75 and the negative ranks add to 3, so W is the total of all ranks, 78, minus twice 3.

steps.title: Tie sum
steps.words: There is one set of size 2 and one set of size 3 among the magnitudes.

steps.title: Tie-corrected standard deviation of W
steps.words: The ties reduce the variance by 2.5, from 650 to 647.5.

steps.title: Compute z_W
steps.words: The mean of W under the null hypothesis is zero, so only the continuity correction is subtracted from |W|.

steps.title: Read the critical value
steps.words: Start with \(\alpha=0.05\). Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 2. In the infinity row and the two-tailed 0.05 column, the printed value is 1.9600.

steps.title: Make the decision and bracket P
steps.words: The statistic exceeds 1.96, so the null hypothesis is rejected. In the infinity row it passes the 0.005 column (2.8070) but not the 0.002 column (3.0902), so 0.002 < P < 0.005.

cases.conclusion: W = 72 and z_W = 2.80987 exceeds 1.9600, so the null hypothesis is rejected (0.002 < P < 0.005). There is a difference in P300 amplitude before and after attention training. The brain response to rare target sounds was larger after four weeks of attention training.

cases.title: Words recalled from sung and spoken lists
cases.context: In a study looking at music and verbal memory, each of twelve adults learned two different 20-word lists, one spoken (measurement 1) and one sung to a simple melody (measurement 2), in random order. Ten minutes after each list the number of words recalled was counted. Word counts are small integers with many ties, so the researchers did not want to assume that the differences are Normally distributed.
tasks: Compute the differences (sung - spoken), drop any zero difference, rank the magnitudes with average ranks for ties, attach the signs and compute W.

Based on the recorded data, is there evidence that the number of words recalled is different in these two conditions? Do not assume that the differences are Normally distributed. Please state how you reached your conclusions.

Provide your result in a single complete sentence that would convey your conclusion in a way that could be understood by a non-expert in statistics or medicine (e.g., a typical reader of a local newspaper).

hypotheses.null: H_0:\text{no difference in words recalled between sung and spoken lists}
hypotheses.alternative: H_A:\text{words recalled differ between sung and spoken lists}
hypotheses.nullWords: There is no difference in the distributions of the number of words recalled between the sung and spoken lists.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The distributions of the number of words recalled differ between the sung and spoken lists.

cases.symbols: \(W\) (sum of the signed ranks), \(n\) (number of nonzero differences), \(\mu_W\) (mean of \(W\) under the null hypothesis), \(\sigma_W\) (standard deviation of \(W\) under the null hypothesis), \(z_W\) (standardized signed-rank sum). \(\tau_i\) (number of tied ranks in the \(i\)th set of ties).

steps.title: State the procedure and hypotheses
steps.words: The same subjects are measured twice, so the procedure is the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. The null hypothesis is that there is no difference in the distributions of the number of words recalled between the sung and spoken lists.

steps.title: Compute the differences
steps.words: Subject 5 has a difference of zero, so it is dropped and n becomes 11. With more than 8 nonzero differences the Normal approximation is used.

steps.title: Rank the magnitudes with ties
general: \text{tied rank}=\text{average of the ranks the tied values occupy}
steps.words: Tied magnitudes share the average of the ranks they occupy, and each rank then takes the sign of its difference. Most magnitudes are 1 or 2, so large tie sets form.

steps.title: Compute W
steps.words: The positive ranks add to 54 and the negative ranks add to 12, so W is the total of all ranks, 66, minus twice 12.

steps.title: Tie sum
steps.words: There are two sets of size 5 among the magnitudes.

steps.title: Tie-corrected standard deviation of W
steps.words: The ties reduce the variance by 20, from 506 to 486.

steps.title: Compute z_W
steps.words: The mean of W under the null hypothesis is zero, so only the continuity correction is subtracted from |W|.

steps.title: Read the critical value
steps.words: Start with \(\alpha=0.05\). Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 2. In the infinity row and the two-tailed 0.05 column, the printed value is 1.9600.

steps.title: Make the decision and bracket P
steps.words: The statistic is below 1.96, so the null hypothesis is not rejected. In the infinity row it passes the 0.10 column (1.6449) but not the 0.05 column (1.9600), so 0.05 < P < 0.10.

cases.conclusion: W = 42 and z_W = 1.88248 is less than 1.9600, so the null hypothesis is not rejected (0.05 < P < 0.10). The data do not show a difference in the number of words recalled between the sung and spoken lists. In this study, people did not remember reliably more or fewer words from a sung list than from a spoken list.

questions.stem: For the pitch-matching errors of the ten trained singers (7, 10, 11, 12, 13, 13, 14, 16, 17, 19 cents), what is the sample SD?
questions.why: The squared deviations from the mean 13.2 add to 111.6. Dividing by n - 1 = 9 gives 12.4, and its square root is 3.52136. Dividing by n, skipping the root, or dividing by the root of n gives the other values.

questions.stem: For the lever presses in extinction (CRF 12, 22, 9, 29, 15 and partial 31, 26, 45, 22, 38, 29, 52), what is the rank sum T of the smaller group?
questions.why: Ranking all twelve counts gives the CRF ranks 1, 2, 3, 4.5 and 7.5, which add to 18. Breaking the ties without averaging gives 17, 60 is the partial group's sum, and 32.5 is the mean of T under the null hypothesis.

questions.stem: For the dizziness ratings of 9 rehabilitation and 11 waitlist patients, the tie sum is 144. What is the tie-corrected standard deviation \(\sigma_T\)?
questions.why: The variance without ties is 9(11)(21)/12 = 173.25, and the ties remove 9(11)(144)/(12(20)(19)) = 3.12632. The root of 170.124 is 13.0431. The other values ignore the ties, forget the root, or subtract the tie sum over 12 as in the signed-rank test.

questions.stem: For the freezing times of 10 mice with extinction training and 12 without, T = 75.5, \(\mu_T=115\) and \(\sigma_T=15.1615\). What is \(z_T\)?
questions.why: The distance 39.5 minus the continuity correction 0.5 is 39, and 39 divided by 15.1615 is 2.57231. The other values skip the correction, use the bigger group's mean, or divide by the variance.

questions.stem: For the tic counts of nine patients before and after habit reversal training, one patient shows no change. What is W (after minus before)?
questions.why: Dropping the zero leaves n = 8. The only positive rank is 1.5 and the negative ranks add to 34.5, so W = 1.5 - 34.5 = -33. Keeping the zero as a rank gives -39, and -34.5 or 1.5 are only one side of the sum.

questions.stem: For the words recalled from sung and spoken lists, W = 42 with n = 11 nonzero differences and a tie sum of 240. What is \(z_W\)?
questions.why: The variance without ties is 11(12)(23)/6 = 506, and the ties remove 240/12 = 20, so \(\sigma_W=\sqrt{486}=22.0454\). Then (42 - 0.5)/22.0454 = 1.88248. The other values ignore the ties, skip the continuity correction, or divide by the variance.

questions.stem: Ten fMRI percent signal change values follow a straight line on a Normal Q-Q plot except one value far above the others, and shapiro.test gives p-value = 0.0001167. Which conclusion fits?
options: Normality is not rejected because nine points follow the line.
Normality is rejected, so a rank-based test is safer for comparing this group.
The data are proven to be Normal because P is small.
The single outlier should be deleted and the t test used without comment.
questions.why: The Shapiro-Wilk null hypothesis is Normality, and P = 0.0001167 is below 0.05, so Normality is rejected. A rank test uses only the order of the values, so one extreme value cannot dominate it.

questions.stem: Spike counts are recorded from 6 neurons in control slices and 11 different neurons in slices bathed in a test solution, and the counts are skewed. How should the two groups be compared?
options: Wilcoxon signed-rank test with the W table
Mann-Whitney rank-sum test with the T table
Paired t test on the counts
Mann-Whitney rank-sum test with the Normal approximation, because n_B = 11 > 8
questions.why: The neurons in the two groups are different, so the rank-sum test applies. The printed T table only covers a bigger group of 8 or fewer, so with 11 the Normal approximation is used.

questions.stem: In a signed-rank test on nine people measured before and after a speech therapy, one person's difference is exactly zero. What happens to that person?
options: The zero difference is dropped, so n = 8 and the W table row n = 8 is used.
The zero gets rank 1 and a positive sign.
The zero is split into half a positive and half a negative rank, and n stays 9.
The whole data set must be analyzed with a paired t test instead.
questions.why: A zero difference carries no sign, so it is removed before ranking and n counts only the nonzero differences.

questions.stem: In a signed-rank test with the Normal approximation, many differences in a word-recall study share the same magnitude. How does the tie correction change the result?
options: It increases \(\sigma_W\), so \(z_W\) gets smaller.
It changes W itself but not \(\sigma_W\).
It reduces \(\sigma_W\), so \(z_W\) gets slightly larger.
It has no effect because ties only matter for the T table.
questions.why: Each tie set subtracts \((\tau_i-1)\tau_i(\tau_i+1)/12\) from the variance, so \(\sigma_W\) shrinks and dividing by it gives a larger z.

notes: All data are invented for practice. Critical values were read from sources/tables/MannWhitney_RankSumT_Table.pdf page 1 (rows n_S = 5, n_B = 7 and n_S = 4, n_B = 7), sources/tables/WilcoxonW_Table.pdf page 1 (rows n = 7 and n = 8) and sources/tables/t_table.pdf page 2 (infinity row, columns 0.50 to 0.001). Each step that reads a table carries tableLookup, and the case lookup repeats the 0.05-level entry, as in the ref cases.

Formula discrepancy (for the reviewer, not stated in the cases). The lecture slide prints the tie term of sigma_T with 12N(N+1) in the denominator. The correct form, used in the ref file and here, is 12N(N-1). The two s24mwnormal cases use N - 1, and the check script confirms the result against SciPy mannwhitneyu (asymptotic, continuity corrected), which uses the same correction.

Wilcoxon W table, row n = 7. Both printed values (28 with P = .016 and 24 with P = .046) have P at most 0.05, so the mood case uses 24 as the 0.05 cutoff and names 28 as the stricter value. The ref cases only show rows n = 6 and n = 8, where one printed P exceeds 0.05.

Printed-table discrepancy (for the reviewer, not stated in the case). In MannWhitney_RankSumT_Table.pdf, row n_S = 4, n_B = 7, the .01 entry is printed as 10,38 with P = .012. The exact two-tailed P of 10,38 is 2/330 = .006, and P = .012 belongs to 11,37 (4/330). The stuttering case records the printed 10,38 (P = .012) faithfully. It does not affect the decision because T = 21.5 is far from both entries.

Outcomes. Reject: lever presses (0.010 < P < 0.048), dizziness (0.005 < P < 0.01), freezing (0.01 < P < 0.02, z just below the 0.01 column value 2.5758), tic counts (P < 0.024), P300 (0.002 < P < 0.005). Do not reject: stuttering therapy (exact P = 0.685), music-session mood (exact P = 0.125), sung versus spoken recall (0.05 < P < 0.10, close to the cutoff). In the two Normality cases, the first group of each is consistent with Normal (P = 0.9951 and P = 0.9917) and the second is rejected.

Following the ref cases of the table methods, a non-rejecting T or W table case states the exact permutation P counted from the actual (tied) ranks. Normal-approximation cases give only a P range from the infinity row.
Ties appear in every rank case. Zero differences are dropped in the tic counts (patient 2), music-session mood (person 2) and sung versus spoken recall (subject 5) cases.

Shapiro-Wilk output was produced by running Rscript (R 4.6.1, shapiro.test on x) on each sample. It is quoted in the third task and stored in full, as R prints it, in values.rOutput1 and values.rOutput2. Values keys added beyond the ref key sets are raw samples (sample1, sample2), group arrays with a groups list naming them (small group first), tie bookkeeping (tieSum, tieSets, varianceNoTies, sigmaTNoTies) and the other printed table entry (critical01, tableP01, critical2).
In the sung versus spoken case the Wilcoxon values keys before and after hold measurement 1 (spoken) and measurement 2 (sung), to keep the ref key names.
The answer of each s24normal case is the Shapiro-Wilk W of the second group, read from the R output as in the ref case.

Colons and semicolons are kept out of words, conclusion and the hypotheses in words. Context and tasks keep the course's exact phrases, including the newspaper sentence with e.g. and the quoted R output line.
